summary:
Earth Information Jukebox is an interactive web experience developed by Angular Lovers to make NASA Earth science more engaging through sight, sound, and exploration.

Inspired by NASA's Earth Information Center, our application transforms real nighttime satellite imagery into music generated in real time. Users can explore an interactive globe, select NASA night-lights images from 2012 or 2023, and listen as visual brightness is translated into musical notes. A synchronized visual indicator and textual descriptions explain how each region contributes to the sound.

Built with Angular, TypeScript, Canvas2D, and the Web Audio API, the project combines scientific visualization with a reproducible sound-generation system. Its purpose is to explore new ways of communicating Earth information, supporting multisensory learning and making complex visual material more approachable.

By turning images into an interactive musical experience, we invite people to discover our changing planet from a different perspective.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Earth Information Jukebox lets people explore a globe and listen to NASA night-lights imagery. It was designed from the start to be a more accessible way to experience Earth science, including for people with low vision. The application opens on the Earth and then offers a separate image-sonification panel. The user chooses the 2012 or the 2023 annual image and presses Play. A highlighted region and a text reading follow the playback, so it is always clear which part of the image is being heard.

HOW IT WORKS

Playback is a spatial scan through one annual image. The relative brightness of the image controls the notes and the gain of the voice, and the horizontal position in the image controls the stereo panorama, so the pattern of the image can be followed by ear as the sound moves between left and right. No audio starts automatically. The sound panel has Play/Pause, Restart, Mute, Volume, Speed and Spatial position controls, and the whole site can be operated from the keyboard.

BENEFITS

NASA's Earth Information Center presents our changing planet mostly through sight. This project offers the same imagery in three forms, image, audio and text, so a person does not need to see fine visual detail to follow the data. The text reading can be used without sound, the highlighted region gives a single clear point of focus instead of a dense map, and comparing 2012 with 2023 becomes something a person can hear as well as see.

INTENDED IMPACT

We want Earth science to reach people who are left out when data is only visual, especially blind and low-vision users, and to give everyone a more engaging, multi-sensory way to experience how human presence on Earth appears from space.

TOOLS AND DATA

- Angular 18 and TypeScript, with HTML and CSS, on Node.js 22, including server-side rendering

- Automated checks: Angular tests in headless Chrome, Node tests and a production smoke test

- Data: two annual night-lights images derived from NASA Scientific Visualization Studio SVS 5276, the original visualization linked by its Earth Information Center version, SVS 5313. A manifest in the repository records the exact resources, hashes, transformation and credits.

- Globe geography from Natural Earth

- [AUDIO TECHNOLOGY, e.g. the browser's Web Audio API or the library used]

- AI assistance was used and is documented in AI_USAGE.md and in the project metadata.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

The project treats the image itself as the score. Instead of placing a soundtrack over a visualization, it reads brightness as melody and loudness and reads geography as stereo space, inside a jukebox where each year is a record to play and compare.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

- An accessible site first: the first keyboard link skips straight to the sound panel; globe destinations, direction buttons and arrow keys select a point; plus/minus change zoom and Home resets the view; reduced motion disables the automatic rotation of the globe.

- User control: sound never starts on its own.

- Honesty about the data: the sound represents RGB image brightness, not calibrated radiance, and black pixels may have several meanings. Globe coordinates do not control the audio, because a geographic transform has not been validated. Source, formulas and limitations are shown in the app under "Method, credits and limitations".

- Credit: NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio and its contributors retain the credits listed in the manifest, and no NASA endorsement is implied.

- Remaining work: human listening tests, screen-reader testing and mobile-device acceptance still need confirmation.
